normalized_decision.output:
Incident Reconstruction. The evidence forms a coherent causal chain. At 09:00 the system operated near baseline: queue depth 120 with 8 workers (E01). By 09:10 the queue had grown more than fifteenfold to 1,850 while the worker count stayed at 8 (E02), indicating that ingress had begun to outpace consumption. Median task latency rose from 1.8 seconds to 14.2 seconds by 09:12 (E03), confirming that workers were spending far longer per task. Critically, at 09:15 outbound dependency B began returning HTTP 429 for 31 percent of requests (E05), the earliest observed external fault and the only evidence of a broken dependency in the chain. Because resource utilization at 09:14 remained moderate (CPU 43 percent, memory 51 percent, disk 22 percent, E04), internal capacity was not exhausted. The most defensible conclusion is that dependency B's rate limiting was the primary cause of the incident, with retry amplification, a fixed worker count, and the absence of circuit breaking acting as amplifiers rather than root causes.

Why the queue formed. When dependency B throttled nearly one third of requests, tasks that depended on B began to block or fail, raising per-task latency (E03) and reducing effective throughput. With a fixed consumer count, the system could no longer drain arrivals, so depth climbed to 1,850 (E02). CPU and memory headroom (E04) shows the workers were waiting on a slow external dependency rather than computing, the classic signature of an I/O-bound bottleneck.

Why adding workers barely helped. At 09:20 the worker count was doubled from 8 to 16, yet queue depth fell only 6 percent over ten minutes (E07). This limited effect is expected when the bottleneck is external: additional workers simply generated more concurrent requests against an already throttled dependency, and each request still waited on or was rejected by B. Adding parallelism cannot remove an external rate limit; it can even aggravate it by increasing the rate at which 429 responses are provoked. This observation strongly discriminates between an internal capacity problem, where doubling workers would materially reduce depth, and an external dependency problem, where it would not.

Retry policy assessment. At 09:16 retry volume increased 420 percent under exponential backoff with a maximum of three retries (E06). The policy was well intentioned but unsafe for this failure mode. Against HTTP 429, retries amplify the very demand that triggered the throttle: each failed request is replayed up to three times, multiplying the request rate toward B while providing no relief. The experimental evidence at 09:26 is decisive: temporarily disabling retries for dependency B caused queue depth to fall 38 percent within six minutes (E08). The policy therefore converted a moderate external degradation into a severe queueing event, and the trade-off was visible: the direct failure rate increased while retries were off (E08), which is the honest cost of avoiding retry storms.

Distinguishing cause from amplifiers. The root cause is dependency B's throttling (E05), corroborated by the recovery evidence: once B's rate limits were raised at 09:35, 429 responses fell below 1 percent and queue depth returned below 150 within eleven minutes (E09). Amplifiers were: first, the retry storm (E06, E08), which added load; second, the fixed worker count early in the incident (E01, E02), which left no headroom to absorb the latency spike; and third, the absence of any circuit breaker, which would have stopped sending work into a throttled dependency. E10 confirms no deploy, schema change, host restart, network route change, or credential rotation between 08:00 and 10:00, eliminating common internal-change causes.

Alternative hypothesis. A plausible alternative is that the incident was caused by internal capacity exhaustion or a slow-consumer regression inside the service. This hypothesis is less supported for three reasons. First, E04 shows CPU, memory, and disk well below saturation at 09:14. Second, E10 rules out deploys and restarts that would accompany a code regression. Third, and most importantly, recovery occurred immediately after the external dependency's rate limits were raised (E09), while internal resources were unchanged. If an internal regression had been the cause, raising B's rate limits would not have cleared the queue. The internal hypothesis therefore fails the intervention test, whereas the external hypothesis passes it.

Uncertainties. Several questions remain open. The evidence does not show why B began throttling, whether due to quota exhaustion, its own upstream degradation, or configuration. The exact end-user error rate during the retry-disabled window is unquantified. It is unknown whether backoff included jitter, and without jitter synchronized retries can form thundering herds. It is also unclear whether the raised rate limits are permanent or temporary. Finally, the absence of queueing details, such as drop policy, priority, and dead-lettering, limits confidence in describing exactly how tasks were affected.

Staged remediation. Stage one, immediate: add a circuit breaker with a half-open probe on the path to dependency B so throttling triggers fast failure instead of queued retries. Stage two, short term: replace fixed maximum retries with a token-budget or adaptive retry policy that includes jitter and Retry-After awareness, treating 429 as non-retryable or narrowly retryable. Stage three: negotiate rate-limit headroom and alert thresholds with the owner of B, and instrument 429 rates as a first-class SLO signal. Stage four: make autoscaling respond to external error rates and latency, not raw queue depth alone, and add load shedding for low-priority work. Stage five: run a game-day exercise replaying a dependency throttle to validate that the system degrades gracefully. Verification for each stage should use queue depth, 429 rate, retry volume, and median latency as the four control metrics (E02, E03, E05, E06).

data.executive_summary: A queue incident occurred between 09:00 and 09:35, driven primarily by external dependency B enforcing rate limits and returning HTTP 429 on roughly one third of requests beginning at 09:15. The immediate queue build-up to 1,850 items and the jump in median latency from 1.8 to 14.2 seconds followed the degradation of dependency B, not internal resource exhaustion; CPU, memory, and disk remained moderate throughout. The retry policy then acted as a powerful amplifier: retry volume rose 420 percent, injecting additional demand into an already saturated path. Scaling workers from 8 to 16 produced only a 6 percent queue reduction, confirming the bottleneck was external. Disabling retries and raising the dependency's rate limits recovered the queue below 150 within eleven minutes. The staged remediation should focus on circuit breaking, retry budget policies, and targeted capacity planning, while an internal capacity hypothesis is plausible but less supported.

findings.claim: At 09:00 the system operated near baseline with queue depth 120 and 8 workers, so the incident began from a healthy state.
The primary cause of the queue incident was outbound dependency B returning HTTP 429 for 31 percent of requests starting at 09:15.
Queue depth rose from 120 to 1,850 within ten minutes while worker count stayed at 8, showing ingress began outpacing consumption.
Median task latency rose from 1.8 seconds to 14.2 seconds by 09:12, indicating tasks were blocked or failing on a slow external call.
Internal resources were not the cause: at 09:14 CPU was 43 percent, memory 51 percent, and disk 22 percent, well below saturation.
The retry policy amplified the incident: retry volume increased 420 percent with exponential backoff and a maximum of three retries, replaying demand into a throttled dependency.
Scaling workers from 8 to 16 at 09:20 reduced queue depth only 6 percent over ten minutes, proving the bottleneck was external to the workers.

Disabling retries for dependency B dropped queue depth 38 percent in six minutes, and after B's rate limits were raised at 09:35, 429s fell below 1 percent and queue depth returned below 150 within eleven minutes, confirming the external dependency as root cause.

risks: Retry storms under a degraded dependency multiply load and extend outages far beyond the original fault.
Blind worker scaling wastes capacity and can worsen throttling by increasing request pressure on the external dependency.
Disabling retries raises the direct failure rate and can degrade the end-user experience during mitigation.
Single-dependency coupling without a circuit breaker allows an external throttle to cascade into unbounded queue growth.
Dependency B's rate limits may degrade again if no capacity agreement or alerting is established.
Median latency of 14.2 seconds represents a severe SLO breach that may trigger customer or SLA impact.
uncertainties: The underlying reason dependency B began returning HTTP 429, such as quota exhaustion, upstream degradation, or misconfiguration, is not shown by the evidence.
The exact end-user error rate during the retry-disabled window at 09:26 is unquantified.
It is unknown whether the exponential backoff included jitter; without jitter, synchronized retries can form thundering herds.
It is unclear whether the raised rate limits on dependency B are permanent or temporary.
Queue details such as drop policy, prioritization, and dead-lettering are unknown, limiting confidence in describing exact task outcomes.

recommendations.action: Add a circuit breaker with a half-open probe on the path to dependency B so throttling triggers fast failure instead of queued retries.
recommendations.rationale: E08 and E09 show the system recovers quickly when requests stop hammering a throttled dependency; fast failure prevents queue buildup.

recommendations.action: Replace the fixed three-retry policy with a token-budget or adaptive retry policy that includes jitter and Retry-After awareness, treating HTTP 429 as non-retryable or narrowly retryable.
recommendations.rationale: E06 and E08 show retries amplified load 420 percent and contributed 38 percent of queue depth; bounded retries with jitter prevent retry storms.

recommendations.action: Negotiate rate-limit headroom and alert thresholds with the owner of dependency B and instrument 429 rates as a first-class SLO signal.
recommendations.rationale: E05 shows throttling appeared without warning; agreements and early alerting reduce time-to-detect on future degradation.

recommendations.action: Make autoscaling respond to external error rates and latency, not raw queue depth alone, and add load shedding for low-priority work.
recommendations.rationale: E07 shows doubling workers yielded only a 6 percent queue reduction, so scaling signals must reflect the actual bottleneck.

recommendations.action: Run a game-day exercise replaying a dependency throttle to validate circuit breaker, retry budget, and load shedding behavior.
recommendations.rationale: Testing the degradation path in advance verifies that mitigation actions match the dynamics observed in E06 through E09.

recommendations.action: Track queue depth, 429 rate, retry volume, and median latency as the four control metrics for post-incident verification.
recommendations.rationale: These four metrics are exactly the signals that diverged in E02, E03, E05, and E06 and together characterize the incident.

alternatives.name: Internal capacity exhaustion or slow-consumer regression
pros: Consistent with a rising queue despite unchanged external inputs
Would explain the limited benefit of the first scaling attempt
cons: Contradicted by moderate CPU, memory, and disk utilization in E04
Contradicted by E10, which rules out deploys and restarts between 08:00 and 10:00
Fails the intervention test: raising B's rate limits cleared the queue without internal changes

alternatives.name: Network partition or route change to dependency B
pros: Could explain widespread request failures toward B
cons: E10 rules out network route changes
HTTP 429 is an application-level throttling response, not a transport failure
Recovery after rate-limit increase is inconsistent with a partition

alternatives.name: Retry storm as the primary cause
pros: Matches the large retry volume increase in E06 and its 38 percent queue contribution in E08
cons: Retries are reactive and require a pre-existing failure; the 429s in E05 preceded the retry surge in E06
Retries cannot initiate the incident, only amplify it

alternatives.name: Downstream consumer slowdown inside the service
pros: Could raise per-task latency and queue depth
cons: Latency rise tracked dependency B's throttling timing in E05
No deploy or configuration change occurred per E10
Worker scaling should have helped a pure compute slowdown, but E07 shows it did not

evidence.observation: At 09:00, queue depth was 120 and worker count was 8.
At 09:10, queue depth rose to 1,850 while worker count remained 8.
At 09:12, median task latency rose from 1.8 seconds to 14.2 seconds.
At 09:14, CPU utilization averaged 43%, memory 51%, and disk utilization 22%.
At 09:15, outbound dependency B began returning HTTP 429 for 31% of requests.
At 09:16, retry volume increased by 420%, using exponential backoff with a maximum of three retries.
At 09:20, increasing worker count from 8 to 16 reduced queue depth only 6% over ten minutes.
At 09:26, temporarily disabling retries for dependency B caused queue depth to fall 38% in six minutes, while direct failure rate increased.
At 09:35, dependency B rate limits were raised and HTTP 429 responses fell below 1%; queue depth then returned below 150 within eleven minutes.
No deploy, schema change, host restart, network route change, or credential rotation occurred between 08:00 and 10:00.

edge_cases: Queue depth at zero or negative, where consumers drain faster than producers enqueue, changing autoscaling semantics
HTTP 429 responses carrying Retry-After headers that are ignored by the retry policy, causing unnecessary replay pressure
Worker scaling beyond available CPU capacity, where added workers contend for shared host resources
Rate limits raised for one tenant while other tenants of dependency B continue consuming shared quota
Simultaneous failure of multiple outbound dependencies, which would invalidate single-dependency attribution
Retries permanently disabled rather than temporarily, leaving failures unhandled and increasing user-visible errors
